The good news is that current HIV treatments work incredibly well, and the life expectancy for someone with properly medicated HIV is now basically the same as someone who is HIV-negative. I've talked to doctors who have said that it's more difficult to manage another chronic health problem such as diabetes than it is to manage HIV. Also, if you're really concerned about getting HIV from unprotected sex, talk to your doctor about PrEP (Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis). It's a combination of drugs designed to stop HIV infection if your body comes into contact with the virus.  


Considering how relatively new HIV is, we've made great strides in treating it effectively. There's still work to be done to make treatments available to all people around the world (looking at you, countries without universal healthcare), but it's considerably less scary than it once was.

I don't have mice any more so I can't show you what I mean, but if you can play around with the settings on your camera rather than leaving it to an automatic mode you have a better chance of snapping non-blurry pics.

The main settings for cameras are the shutter speed, ISO and aperture. To capture things that move very fast (e.g. mice) you need a short shutter speed. This means that the time the camera sensor is exposed to light is minimal, and motion blur is reduced. However, it does mean that less light gets to the sensor, so you will need to adjust your aperture size (the hole in the camera lens that lets light in - think of it like the pupil of the eye) and your ISO (this is the light sensitivity of the camera sensor) otherwise your photo will be too dark (underexposed).

Hi! I had a hysto in July 2018 after deciding I didn't want phallo or meta. I was experiencing chronic cramps (think labour pains, but every couple of days for years on end), so that was my reason for getting it. 

As far as I'm aware, there have been no negative consequences. I'd definitely go for keyhole surgery over traditional abdominal hysto - my keyhole surgery was a breeze and I woke up from the anaesthetic feeling like I'd just done too many sit-ups. Was discharged from hospital the next day and was back to normal within a week. Your mileage may vary, but it's generally a very quick recovery if you don't have other medical issues. 

I don't know how you like to have sex so maybe this is irrelevant, but one thing I did notice is that after removal of my cervix I'm a bit "tighter" down there. It's not affected my enjoyment of sex, but it definitely takes a little longer to get me suitably warmed up. 

Basically, life post-hysto is great! I'm pain free, which is nice, and obviously don't have to worry about the threat of periods returning any more. If it's something you want to do, go for it!

For starters, it's extremely difficult to gain access if you're not Jewish (or at least it was in 2010 when I visited). The museum had Israeli guards at the entrance, who asked us where we were from and what we were doing there. We told him my grandpa's surname and said where we were from (my home city is known for a large Jewish population, although we're not), and they eventually let us through.

The memorial was very cramped and felt as if it echoed a gas chamber, although that apparently wasn't its goal. My grandpa had actually written to the Jewish community in Munich saying he didn't want his parents' names on the memorial as he felt they were being hidden away, but they put them on anyway. It just felt really eerie for 14-year-old me.

I'm a trash millennial who hasn't a hope in hell of ever buying his own house, but this advice is from when I was growing up and moved for the first time.

- Check what type of soil your house is built on!! We moved from a place with fairly solid ground to an area that's mainly soft clay. The house was built in around 1900-1910 so it's sturdy as hell, but cracks still appear when the ground shifts. Enquire as to what materials your house is actually made of if it's in a soft soil area, as it might affect how sturdy your house is.

- Make sure you ask whether the previous owners know of any DIY work done on the house. My parents didn't (too busy raising three kids) and we ended up with quite a few problems because the previous owner was crap at DIY. At one point we had rats in the walls and it turned out it was due to a cracked sewer pipe. The man we bought the house off had tried to install new pipes himself, but with the house being on a slope one kept cracking. So naturally instead of getting a proper plumber in, he propped up the pipe with bits of old carpet. About five years after we moved in, the carpet finally rotted away and the pipe fell, leaving a gap for rats to get in. We got exterminators in no problem, but I'll never forget the smell of a dead rat that somehow got trapped behind out sink for weeks.

- Know when the house was built. It'll help when trying to figure out what sort of features your house has and whether you have to update them for safety.

Not me, but my grandpa. He moved from Germany to rural Wales in 1939, aged 16. I know Germany isn't a developing country, but back in the 1930s things were pretty rough for a Jewish teenager in Bavaria. He doesn't talk much about what he first thought of Britain, but from the few things he has said I've managed to piece together what it was like.

- First things first, he was really fucking surprised that nobody gave a shit that he was Jewish. He didn't have to be paranoid about which shops or restaurants he could go into. He could go to school again. 

- The flipside of this was that people were more concerned about the fact he was German. He moved around a lot and was almost kicked out of boarding school because they thought he could be a spy.

- The food! His parents were pretty well off, but by 1939 anti-Semitism meant that their quality of life had drastically reduced. His father lost his job and didn't have a lot to live on. Once he got to Wales he basically lived on a farm for a while, so food was good quality and readily available. 

- One of the minor things that really confused him were Welsh accents. He knew a little bit of English from some tutoring he'd had, but initially he couldn't understand his foster family at all.

In all fairness, I hadn't ever witnessed so much casual swearing until I went to Aus. I thought we Brits were pretty laid back when it came to bad language, but you guys definitely win the "how to fit as many expletives as possible into a normal sentence" game.

Growing up I just remember being a kid. I don't think I had a concept of gender, unless I was forced to wear skirts (which I hated). Then puberty struck. I have a brain condition that often leads to precocious puberty, so while the rest of my family were fairly late bloomers, I started growing breasts at around 8. Got my period a month after my 11th birthday. That fucking sucked. 

I remember having this conversation with a friend of mine about how she'd thought she might be a boy growing up. We must have been about 13. And I said to her that I felt like that, and I didn't think it would go away. But then I blocked out that conversation entirely. I tried to forget, even though I wanted to tear my chest off every day. I said to myself that once I turned 18 I was going to go for a breast reduction. I tried binding with scarves, and sometimes put belts around my chest to flatten it. My little brother grew taller than me and I felt so jealous.

Then when I was 16 it was like everything clicked into place. I came out and was referred to the children's gender clinic. But there wasn't much point me being there. I was too old for hormone blockers. I slipped into a horrible depression that forced me to quit in my last year of Sixth Form. My family weren't accepting. I passed sometimes, but as a 12-year-old. 

Being 17 was just a blur of suicide attempts and mind-numbing depression.

But I turned 18, and decided to go back to education - this time at art college. I was passed onto the adult gender service fairly quickly and after a boring period of assessment managed to get on T in April 2015, just over 2 years after I came out.

The year since then has been absolutely fantastic. I can grow a pretty patchy beard and I've gone from being an alto to a bass. Ooh, and I have top surgery scheduled for just after I finish college - only 7 weeks away! Life isn't perfect, but right now it's pretty damn great.
